title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search
hook: One long search trajectory can't be both deep and wide at once. WebSwarm lets the search tree grow instead: any node that can't solve its own piece just spawns children and waits for their evidence.
key_points: Each agentic search node holds a local objective plus a search mode describing how it should search and collaborate.
A node either solves its objective directly or delegates to child nodes, which pass evidence back up the tree.
Probes how relevant information is organized on the web first, to ground how nodes expand.
Reuses process-level experience across sibling nodes tackling similar sub-objectives instead of relearning from scratch.
Outperforms single-agent and multi-agent baselines on BrowseComp-Plus, WideSearch, DeepWideSearch, and GISA.
content_html: A single web-search agent has to choose between going deep on one thread or wide across many — one long trajectory can't easily do both. WebSwarm lets the search tree grow instead: any node that can't solve its own piece just spawns children and waits for their evidence.
extra_html:
How it works

WebSwarm dynamically instantiates agentic search nodes, each holding a local objective plus a search mode describing how it should search and collaborate. A node either answers its objective directly or delegates to child nodes; once children resolve, their evidence and results flow back up so the parent can expand further, revise its approach, or aggregate everything into an answer. To make expansion smarter, WebSwarm first probes how relevant information tends to be organized on the web, and it reuses process-level experience across sibling nodes tackling similar sub-objectives instead of relearning from scratch each time.

Why it matters

Tested on BrowseComp-Plus, WideSearch, DeepWideSearch, and GISA — benchmarks spanning deep, wide, and mixed deep-and-wide research tasks — WebSwarm consistently beats both single-agent and existing multi-agent baselines. The authors' ablations point to the recursive delegation and sibling-experience reuse as the parts doing the real work, rather than just throwing more parallel agents at the problem. Song, Zhang, and colleagues (Renmin University, Kuaishou), arXiv 2026.

flashcards.prompt: What structural limit does WebSwarm address in web-search agents?
flashcards.back_html: A single ReAct-style agent is stuck with one long trajectory and limited context, making it hard to be both deep (thorough on one thread) and wide (broad coverage) at once.

flashcards.prompt: What does a WebSwarm search node do when it can't resolve its own local objective?

choices.text: It spawns child nodes and later aggregates their returned evidence to make progress on its objective
It gives up and returns an empty result to its parent
It restarts the entire search from the root node

flashcards.explanation_html: Nodes progressively delegate: a stuck node creates children, and their evidence flows back up so the parent can expand, revise, or aggregate.

flashcards.prompt: How does WebSwarm avoid treating every search node as a totally independent search?
flashcards.back_html: It reuses process-level experience across sibling nodes facing similar sub-objectives, rather than having each node search entirely from scratch.
